Sumimi v0.4.3 — **the same code, the measurement repeated, and the numbers
corrected**.

**What this is.** No code change. The memory work of v0.4.2 was measured
again — twice on the Linux box, three times on the Apple M5, back to back,
with the released binaries — and two things came out of it that the v0.4.2
notes did not say:

* the deployment table was measured on the Mac, whose peak figure does not
  repeat from one round to the next; it is now measured on the Linux box,
  whose peak is the kernel's exact high-water mark;
* the allocator is **not free**. It gives back 12–21% of the peak, and it
  costs about 5% of the throughput.

**The peak, measured on a 2 vCPU Linux box** (the exact high-water mark — the
server reads its own `/proc` figure; a fresh server per row; 64 connections;
20 seconds a point):

| the rate offered | v0.4.1 | **v0.4.2** | **v0.4.2 + the allocator** |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 5 000 /s | 136 / 138 MB | 138 / 138 MB | **110 / 111 MB** |
| 10 000 /s | 145 / 146 MB | 145 / 146 MB | **115 / 115 MB** |
| 20 000 /s | 221 / 234 MB | **208 / 208 MB** | **182 / 183 MB** |
| 40 000 /s | 221 / 239 MB | **210 / 210 MB** | **178 / 186 MB** |

Two runs each, so the numbers are not one lucky run. The same box, the same
tool, back to back:

* the CPU-bound box **serves 17% more traffic** (16 812 → 19 724 requests a
  second) — the batching made three transactions out of a thousand requests,
  and the ceiling was the CPU;
* at the same rate the peak is **−9%**;
* with the allocator the peak is **−12% to −21%**.

**The allocator costs 5% of the throughput.** `mmap`/`munmap` are system
calls: the pages come back to the operating system, and the CPU pays for
them. It is a knob, not a free win — the Docker image sets it, and a systemd
deployment should set it in the environment file:

```bash
MALLOC_MMAP_THRESHOLD_=65536
```

A box that is short of memory should set it even if it could spare the 5%.

**It does nothing on macOS.** The variable is glibc's; on macOS and the BSDs
the allocator is different, and the measurement shows it: with and without
it, the Mac reads 139 / 147 / 246 / 270 MB. The server is fine there — it
just does not need the help.

**One number to be careful with.** The Mac's figure is the kernel's
`ru_maxrss`, which counts the shared pages of the mapped binary and does not
repeat from one round to the next: the same binary at 5 000 requests a
second measured 104 MB in one round and 133 MB in the next, while the Linux
figure repeated to within 2 MB. **The deployment table is a Linux table**, and
the measurement workflow runs on a Linux runner for the same reason.

**The rule, corrected.** The v0.4.2 notes said the peak was "68 MB + 1.2 MB
per 1 000 requests a second". That was not what the table said. What the
repeated measurement shows is a **flat curve**: between 5 000 and 10 000
requests a second the peak grows by **1 MB per 1 000** (it used to grow by
7.8 MB), and then it stops — **182 MB whether you offer 20 000 or 40 000**.
The lowest few MB are the batch waiting to be written, which is a constant,
not a slope. So on that box the limit is now the **CPU**, not the memory.

**Nothing changed for the user.** Same binaries as v0.4.2, same API, same
tracker, same reports. The documentation page that ships with this release
carries the corrected tables and the note about the cost.

```bash
sumimi serve --dir ./sumimi --port 3000
```
